cases.interviewerQuestion: Since Chrome extensions can't share cookies with your main app's domain, walk me through how you designed the bearer-token auth flow — how did you handle token issuance and refresh without a shared session store?
cases.tonyRaw:
I solo-owned this surface, so the design decisions were mine end to end. Since the extension runs on its own origin, cookies from the main app were never an option — I issued a bearer token at login that the extension stored and attached as an Authorization header on every request into the backend, rather than trying to piggyback on the web app's session cookie. For refresh, I avoided standing up a shared session store by keeping the token validation stateless on the backend — the tradeoff there is you lean more on token expiry/reissue logic client-side than on server-side revocation, which is a real limitation I'd flag if this were handling something more sensitive than what Product Forge needed.

That auth layer was also the foundation for the other ~30 route handlers I built for artifact/meeting CRUD and the Liveblocks passthrough, since all of those needed the same bearer-token check on every request.

cases.interviewerQuestion: When you were both learning Spanner and Dataflow from scratch, what was the first major assumption from your SQL background that broke once you started designing the schema and migration pipeline for Spanner's distributed model?
cases.tonyRaw: The big one was primary key design — with traditional SQL you get comfortable with monotonically increasing IDs and let the database handle ordering for you, but in Spanner that pattern creates hotspotting because of how it splits data across nodes. We had to rethink key structure to distribute writes evenly instead of relying on sequential IDs. cases.interviewerQuestion: When you first noticed the stale-state bugs, what made you realize the root cause was architectural—mixing these three kinds of state in one store—rather than something you could patch with better memoization or selector logic?
cases.tonyRaw: I tried the patching route first, honestly — added selectors, tweaked memoization, chased down re-render triggers. But the bugs kept resurfacing in different shapes, and that pattern is usually the tell: if fixing a symptom in one place just moves it somewhere else, you're not looking at a bug, you're looking at a structural mismatch. What clinched it was noticing the three kinds of state had fundamentally different lifecycles and consistency guarantees — Liveblocks data is eventually-consistent and multiplayer, server data needs invalidation semantics, local UI state is synchronous and single-consumer — and no amount of selector logic fixes that when they're all sitting in one undifferentiated store fighting each other's update timing.

cases.interviewerQuestion: When you were designing the state-management layer to inject AI output into ProseMirror's typed node model, what was the trickiest edge case you hit reconciling generated content with the existing document schema — and how did supporting two concurrent editor versions complicate that?
cases.tonyRaw: The trickiest part was that AI-generated content doesn't naturally arrive as valid ProseMirror nodes — you get text/structure that has to be mapped into the typed schema without violating node invariants, so I had to build a reconciliation step that validated and transformed generated output before it ever touched editor state, rather than trusting it directly. Supporting two concurrent editor versions made this worse because the schema itself wasn't identical across versions, so the state-management layer couldn't assume a single fixed node structure — it had to branch or normalize against whichever schema was live. I co-led a team of 3 to 4 engineers on this feature and personally designed that state-management layer integrating AI output into the document model, which is where most of the edge-case handling lived.

cases.interviewerQuestion: Walk me through what actually breaks when you feed a long meeting transcript into an LLM without chunking — was this a hard context-window ceiling, or more of a quality degradation as you approached it, and how did that shape where you put the chunk boundaries?
cases.tonyRaw: It was more quality degradation than a hard wall — you could technically stuff a long transcript in, but the model would start losing track of earlier speakers, conflating decisions made at different points, or just flattening nuance the longer the input got. So the chunk boundaries weren't driven purely by token limits; I put them at natural conversational breaks — topic shifts, speaker transitions — rather than fixed-size splits, because arbitrary cutoffs mid-discussion made downstream summarization worse, not better. I was contributing to an existing agentic assistant here, not architecting it from scratch — my piece was specifically that chunking and context-window handling so it held up reliably on long meetings, plus some tool-selection prompting work on top of it.

cases.interviewerQuestion: When you were tuning the debounce delay over those nine months, what signals told you the timing was wrong—were you chasing user complaints, watching save conflicts, or something else entirely?
cases.tonyRaw: It was mostly save conflicts and stale-state bugs surfacing in actual usage, not user complaints — Product Forge had a small user base, so I didn't have a big complaint pipeline to chase. What I was watching was dirty-state tracking against save timing: if the delay was too short, I'd see redundant saves firing off rapid edits; too long, and you'd get a bigger window where a user could navigate away or trigger another action before a save landed. So it was iterative — adjust the delay, watch how dirty-state and save calls behaved under normal editing patterns, and tighten it from there.

cases.interviewerQuestion: When you were designing the data model, what were the trickiest tradeoffs in shaping schemas that had to serve both the GraphQL API layer and whatever underlying trading data stores already existed?
cases.tonyRaw: The tricky part was that the underlying trading data wasn't shaped for public consumption — it existed in stores optimized for internal trading operations, not for exposing curated, performant profile data to a GraphQL layer. I was part of a team that built the Trader Public Profile platform, and I contributed to the data model design specifically around figuring out where to draw the line between reshaping data at the API resolver level versus pushing structure further back into the underlying stores. Since I didn't own this end to end, my focus was mainly on getting the schema decisions right for the GraphQL layer and UI needs while staying aligned with the rest of the team on how much transformation logic should live upstream versus at the API boundary.
